newsitem.title: GERMANY: Zwickel sees no sense for German jobs talk - paper.
newsitem.headline: Zwickel sees no sense for German jobs talk - paper.

text.p: The leader of Germany's powerful IG Metall union said he saw no sense in a new summit with Chancellor Helmut Kohl on the country's persistent jobless problem, a newspaper reported on Wednesday.

Klaus Zwickel told Germany's Bild Zeitung in an interview that he would refuse to attend any new round of talks in the so-called "Alliance for Jobs" proposed by Kohl to deal with Germany's record four million unemployed workers.
But Zwickel said he would still travel to Bonn to discuss the unemployment crisis -- the jobless level rose to about four million workers in December -- with government leaders.
"I see at the moment on the whole no reason to resume the old round," Zwickel told the mass-circulation newspaper. "Talks in the old form are senseless after our bitter experiences."

The unions felt let down by the collapse last year of the first round of jobs talks, under which unions offered wage moderation in return for pledges from employers and government to tackle Germany's chronic unemployment.

Intense friction emerged after Kohl last year introduced a 70 billion mark austerity package aimed at whipping Bonn's finances into shape for European currency union in 1999 which included cuts in sick pay benefits and job protection laws.

Zwickel told the newspaper that the proposals in the first round would have "finally done something against the massive unemployment problems" but that "not one job has been created and instead the situation has been devastated" due to the collapse of the talks.

"We remain on the offensive: Overtime must be radically reduced and work hours further shortened. There must also be public and private investment for new jobs. We will put pressure on both employers and the government," Zwickel said.
He also said Kohl's publicly-announced goal to halve unemployment by the year 2000 must be realised and said lower interest rates would help spur investment to create new jobs.
"The government must return to creating an attractive work market," he told the newspaper.
